Online romance scams are among the oldest deceptions on the internet, yet fresh victims continue to fall for them. A joint study by four universities has shown that AI chatbots are now capable of running these scams even more effectively than real people — a prospect that is genuinely alarming.

網上情緣騙案

Modern romance scams typically begin on dating apps. Scammers reach out to victims using a highly attractive profile, playing the role of an ardent suitor who ticks every box on the victim's wish list.

They engage victims in lengthy online conversations that usually last for months. Their go-to excuse for being unable to meet in person is that they are on an extended trip overseas.

Eventually one of two things happens: either they claim to have run into an emergency and urgently need money wired to help them out of trouble, or the conversation shifts to what they describe as a lucrative investment, persuading the victim to pour funds into a bogus cryptocurrency scheme.

These scams earn the label "long cons" precisely because they rely on building trust over time — victims and scammers often chat every single day for months on end. Although it may look like a huge time investment, the operations are typically run out of scam compounds in places like Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos, where the workers earn extremely low wages and are, in many cases, trafficking victims forced into the job.

AI 對真人

A study reported by Wired magazine put ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini through their paces.

Researchers from India's Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Venice's Foscari University, the University of Melbourne and Ben Gurion University of the Negev [...] pitted AI chatbots directly against humans, simulating an entire scam operation — more specifically, the kind of conversation designed to build trust over the long haul and ultimately nudge the target into a fake investment. The findings [...] showed the AI chatbots were remarkably effective: not only did they convincingly pass for human, they even outperformed the actual human "scammers" in the experiment on certain metrics.

The test subjects had no idea what the study was really about — whether they were chatting with a real person or an AI, they all believed they were talking to a human. The researchers measured the level of trust built up using both subjective and objective tests. When asked at the end to download an app, only 18% of those who had been chatting with a real person agreed — but among those who had been talking to an AI chatbot, nearly half went ahead and did it.

On top of that, when participants were asked to rate how much they trusted their conversation partner, the AI bots scored noticeably higher.

呢項技術可以令騙案規模大幅擴張

The most worrying implication of the research is that scam centres swapping human operators for AI chatbots could massively scale up their operations. In theory, an AI scam bot could be chatting with thousands of victims simultaneously.

Human intervention would only be needed at the final stage — when the victim is asked to hand over money — in order to bypass the safety guardrails built into AI systems.
